column3: Repeats the elite rejection of a human messenger and adds their appeal to ordinary eating and drinking.
Extends the forefather reference into resurrection skepticism, though not inherited hearing itself.
Reiterates the same ancestor-and-resurrection objection with little beyond 56:48.
Closely parallels elite rejection of Noah as human and adds contempt for his low-status followers.
Supplies Noah's monotheistic call that provokes the elite response in the focus ayah.
Counters ancestral authority by placing the present community and its forefathers under one Lord.
Directly pairs dismissal of clear signs with the claim that predecessors never heard this message.
Offers a positive frame in which God is Lord of both the audience and their first forefathers.
Combines the human-messenger objection, resistance to ancestral worship, and a demand for proof.
Directly repeats the claim that divine sending should have come through angels.
The immediate continuation shows the elite adding a charge of madness to their dismissal.
Denies that being earlier grants superiority, addressing the status premise behind the elite's accusation.
Shows opponents calling the messenger a man who seeks to turn people from ancestral worship.
Immediately states that obeying a human like themselves is treated as loss.
Exposes an escalating demand for a familiar proof as a pretext after prior revelation was also rejected.
The messengers accept their shared humanity while locating their commission and signs in God's favor.
Uses forefathers in a different resurrection objection rather than as an inherited-hearing standard.
The fate of persistent disbelief does not clarify the focus's objections to messengerhood.
Nearly repeats the claim that what was not heard in an inherited religious setting is fabricated.
Records Noah's immediate appeal for help in response to the rejection just voiced.
Its inaccessible report of the high assembly only distantly counters the charge of fabricated speech.
Pairs the human-like-us objection with the accusation that the message is visible magic.
A later prayer about promised punishment does not add to the elite's stated reasoning.
General rejection of witnessed signs does not specify the human, angelic, or ancestral objections.
The same community recasts a promise known from forefathers as tales of the ancients.
Repeats the ancestor-and-resurrection formulation with little marginal help after 23:83.
The alternation of night and day does not illuminate the focus's dispute.
Shows revelation being dismissed as imitable speech and tales of the ancients, extending the archival dismissal.
The next local objection makes explicit the resurrection claim underlying this community's resistance.
Divine hearing and sight in Moses' encounter does not clarify the focus ayah.
Sets later disbelief within a conflict where the weak blame the arrogant for blocking belief.
The assurance of eventual punishment adds no new account of the objection.
Granted distinction and provision concern communal favor, only indirectly related to claimed self-exaltation.
Angels as guardians do not address the demand for angelic messengers.
Directly contrasts following revelation with following the path found among forefathers.
Recasts the human-messenger objection through a political hierarchy in which their people serve the objectors.
The opposition between repentance and desire is unrelated to the focus.
The local dismissal of the promised future continues the rejection but adds no messenger criterion.
The difficult day of summons is consequence material, not an account of the focus's objections.
God's Lordship over first forefathers is a broad antecedent parallel already supplied more directly.
Calling Noah's episode a sign and test supplies only a general narrative frame.
The label tales of the ancients is a related way to neutralize a present divine message.
Directly answers that a messenger can be human like the audience while receiving revelation.
Cosmic Lordship does not address the focus's specific claims.
The acceptance of good deeds has no material connection to the elite's reasoning.
God's ability to make angels on earth only loosely bears on the requested angelic descent.
The local denial of resurrection is secondary to the focus's objection to the messenger.
Demanding the forefathers be brought back is a different evidentiary use of ancestry.
Repeats the human recipient of revelation without adding beyond 41:6.
A later trait of believers does not clarify the earlier elite's objections.
Retribution for deeds is not a meaningful parallel to the focus.
Divine differentiation among messengers weakly distinguishes God's favor from the elite's charge of self-promotion.
The dream scene does not bear on the focus ayah.
The paternal name and condemnation have no relevant explanatory link.
The conditional divine-will formula occurs in a military setting, not messenger selection.
The local accusation now explicitly calls the human messenger a liar against God.
Creation and polytheism do not sharpen the focus's human or ancestral objections.
Questioning God's intended parable is only a broad parallel in hostile reception of revelation.
Explicitly identifies their speech as repetition of what the earlier people said.
The description of ritual practice is unrelated to the focus.
Hostility to revelation descending on others gives a distant counterpart to the elite's threatened status.
Divine power to replace a creation is too general to explain the focus's stated demands.
The demand to produce ancestors is another resurrection challenge, not a claim about inherited hearing.
An elite council's logistical request does not illuminate the rejecting council in the focus.
Noah's renewed plea for help marks the immediate consequence of the community's denial.
Directly joins human likeness, denial of divine sending, and the charge of lying.
Explains why earthly human communities receive human messengers rather than angels.
Protection from devils is unrelated to the elite's arguments.
The legal expiation and its warning to disbelievers do not clarify the focus.
Distorting words and professing disobedient hearing only loosely contrasts with inherited hearing.
The destruction of earlier peoples gives a broad historical consequence, not the focus's reasoning.
Mentioning mother and father has no connection to ancestral authority in the focus.
A queen consulting her assembly about a letter does not clarify elite rejection.
The predicted regret is the immediate divine answer to the deniers in this narrative.
The Adam-Jesus comparison does not address the focus's messenger criteria.
Restates Noah's call and warning, providing the parallel mission that the focus's elite reject.
Instructions to messengers later in the surah do not explain this rejection scene.
The fate of Satan and followers is not a useful parallel to the focus.
Hearing and obeying a covenant provides only a distant positive contrast to refusal of a new report.
Following earlier peoples with later ones gives only a general sequence of generations.
Affirms that a present teaching may already stand in earlier scriptures, challenging the no-prior-hearing premise.
Guidance through earlier practices does not address the focus's specific objections.
The rise of later generations supplies a broad continuation of the narrative cycle.
Directly asks whether they rejected the discourse because it had not come to their first forefathers.
The non-descent of an angelic army after punishment only remotely resembles the angel claim.
The local question whether they know their messenger offers an alternative diagnosis for their denial.
Names Pharaoh's elite as arrogant and exalted, sharpening the status dynamic behind the focus's objection.
Elite consultation alone is too generic to add to the rejecting assembly.
Repeats the bodily-resurrection objection with no inherited-hearing or messenger dimension.
A group from the earlier people does not bear on the focus.
An excessive demand for a book from heaven parallels the insistence on extraordinary heavenly proof.
The condemnation of human ingratitude does not clarify the focus's claims.
Rules about eating in relatives' homes are unrelated to the focus.
Public wealth makes status appear desirable, offering a social backdrop for fear of another's elevation.
The warning not to deny another's faith for worldly gain is only indirectly related to status-driven judgment.
Being among the first believers weakly reverses the value assigned to being among the earlier people.
The challenge to false protectors and creation rivals does not illuminate the focus's objections.
The arrival of clear evidence amid disbelief is too general after the more exact reception parallels.
Identifying Jonah as a messenger adds no relevant detail.
General self-wronging through denial of signs is a remote consequence of the focus's disbelief.
Directly makes inherited ancestral practice the stated reason for refusing what God revealed.
Closely repeats the appeal to what forefathers followed as sufficient against revelation and knowledge.
Directly voices the demand that an angel should have been sent with the messenger.
Explains that an angelic messenger would still have been presented in human form to human hearers.
The messenger explicitly disclaims being an angel, distinguishing revelation from angelic identity.
Shows a people defending a practice because they found their forefathers doing it.
Frames the arrival of a reminder through a man from the community as a cause of wonder.
Reiterates the question whether a reminder sent through a man from among them should be surprising.
Combines the call to abandon ancestral worship with resistance to a sole divine authority.
Identifies revelation to a man from the people as the very thing objectors find astonishing.
Combines refusal to leave ancestral practice with the accusation that the two messengers seek greatness in the land.
Directly reports the demand for an angel to accompany the messenger as a visible proof.
Shows a community resisting a prophet because his call would abandon what their forefathers worshiped.
Affirms that the messengers sent before were men from human communities who received revelation.
Places earlier messengers within ordinary human family life, reinforcing their human condition.
Directly challenges the messenger to bring angels if he is truthful.
Answers that angels are not sent down merely to satisfy such a challenge.
States the recurring pattern that God sent men to whom revelation was given.
Includes the demand for an angelic guarantee and answers it with the messenger's human, sent status.
Names the claim that God sent a human messenger as the barrier to belief.
Explicitly states that the messengers sent before were men receiving revelation.
Adds that those earlier human messengers lived ordinary embodied lives rather than being immortal beings.
Makes found ancestral worship the community's direct explanation for its religious allegiance.
Objects that the messenger eats food and walks in markets and demands an accompanying angel.
Directly asks why angels were not sent down and why God was not visibly seen.
States that the people persist in worship simply because they found their fathers doing it.
Directly rejects a prophet as only a human being like the audience.
Repeats the human-like-us objection in another prophetic confrontation.
Describes a people following their fathers despite finding those fathers astray.
Shows disbelievers treating the rise of a warner from among them as a startling and suspect claim.
Turns the messenger's selection into a status objection by asking why the reminder came to him among them.
Directly asserts that inherited forefather practice supplies both religion and guidance.
Specifically attributes this ancestral defense to affluent elites when a warner comes to a town.
Tests whether inherited practice should still govern when a better-guiding revelation arrives.
Explicitly objects that the Quran was not sent to a great man from one of the two towns.
Counters elite control over rank by locating the distribution of livelihood and degrees with God.
Rejects following a single human from among the people as error and madness.
Names the rejection of human guides as the reason earlier communities disbelieved.
